title: What are PM2.5, PM10 and NO2?
summary: Learn how these microscopic pollutants enter your body — from your nose to your bloodstream.
content: PM2.5 are fine particles smaller than 2.5 micrometers — about 30 times thinner than a human hair. They bypass your nose and throat and penetrate deep into your lungs. PM10 particles (up to 10 micrometers) are filtered partly by your nose and throat but can still reach your bronchial tubes. NO2 (nitrogen dioxide) comes from vehicle exhaust and industrial burning. It irritates the airways and can trigger asthma attacks. Once inhaled, PM2.5 particles can enter your bloodstream and reach your heart, brain, and other organs.

title: How air pollution affects your body
summary: A body-map look at how pollution impacts lungs, heart, brain, eyes, and skin.
content: Lungs: Pollution irritates and inflames airways, reducing lung capacity over time. Heart: Fine particles entering the bloodstream can trigger inflammation, narrowing arteries and raising heart attack risk. Brain: Studies link long-term pollution exposure to cognitive decline and increased stroke risk. Eyes: High pollution causes redness, watering, and can worsen conditions like conjunctivitis. Skin: Airborne particles clog pores and accelerate skin aging and can trigger eczema flare-ups.

title: Health effects by exposure
summary: Short-term: coughs and irritation. Long-term: lung and heart disease.
content: Short-term effects (hours to days): eye irritation, coughing, throat irritation, worsening of asthma and bronchitis, reduced lung function. Long-term effects (years): chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), lung cancer, cardiovascular disease, reduced life expectancy. Children who grow up in high-pollution areas develop smaller lung capacity. Elderly and those with pre-existing conditions face higher risk at all exposure levels.

title: What should I do?
summary: Actions by AQI band: masks, staying indoors, purifiers, ventilation.
content:
Good (0–50): No precautions needed. Enjoy outdoor activity.
Satisfactory (51–100): Generally safe. Sensitive people may want to avoid heavy exertion.
Moderate (101–200): Unusually sensitive people should consider reducing exertion. Keep windows closed during peak traffic hours.
Poor (201–300): Everyone should reduce prolonged outdoor exertion. Wear N95 mask outdoors. Run a purifier if available.
Very Poor (301–400): Avoid all outdoor exertion. Keep windows closed. N95 mask essential outdoors.
Severe (401+): Stay indoors. Keep windows and doors sealed. Run purifier on max. Visit a doctor if symptoms develop.

title: Why Delhi gets bad in winter
summary: Stubble burning, temperature inversion, Diwali firecrackers, and traffic — the perfect storm.
content:
Every October–November, Delhi faces some of the world's worst air quality. Four main reasons:
1. Stubble burning: Farmers in Punjab and Haryana burn leftover crop stubble — releasing smoke that drifts into Delhi.
2. Temperature inversion: Cold air traps a warm air layer above the city, acting like a lid that traps pollutants near the ground.
3. Diwali firecrackers: A single night of firecrackers can spike PM2.5 by 5–10 times over the base level.
4. Traffic and industry: In winter, calm winds and cold air reduce pollutant dispersal, making everyday emissions accumulate faster.

title: Myths vs Facts
summary: Common misconceptions about air quality — debunked with evidence.
content:
Myth: Cloth masks protect against PM2.5. Fact: Standard cloth masks filter only 10–20% of fine PM2.5 particles. N95 masks filter 95%+ when properly fitted.
Myth: You can see when air is polluted. Fact: Some of the most harmful gases (NO2, CO) are invisible and odorless.
Myth: Indoor air is always safer. Fact: Indoor air can be 2–5x more polluted than outdoor air due to cooking, cleaning products, and inadequate ventilation.
Myth: Trees completely solve air pollution. Fact: Trees help at a city scale over decades, but they cannot clean severely polluted air fast enough to protect you today.
Myth: Air pollution only affects your lungs. Fact: As covered above, it affects your heart, brain, eyes, and skin too.
